```{r message=FALSE}
# --- 1. SETUP: Load Libraries ---
# Load only the packages we need for this workflow
# 'tidyverse' loads ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, and tibble all at once
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(tidyverse) 
library(FSA) # For Dunn's Test

# --- 2. LOAD DATA (Read each file only ONCE) ---

# --- Read OTU Table ---
otu_raw <- read.table("kohler.opti_mcc.0.03.subsample.shared", header = TRUE, sep = "\t")
otu_mat <- otu_raw[, -(1:3)]
rownames(otu_mat) <- otu_raw$Group 
otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)
otu_tab <- otu_table(otu_mat, taxa_are_rows = TRUE)

# --- Read and Process Taxonomy ---
tax_raw <- read.table("kohler.opti_mcc.0.03.cons.taxonomy", sep = "\t", header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, quote = "")
taxonomy_strings <- tax_raw$Taxonomy
names(taxonomy_strings) <- tax_raw$OTU

taxonomy_clean <- lapply(strsplit(taxonomy_strings, ";"), function(x) {
    x <- x[nchar(x) > 0]                # Remove empty strings
    x <- gsub("\\(.*?\\)|\\\"", "", x) # Remove confidence scores and quotes
    trimws(x)                           # Trim whitespace
})

max_ranks <- 7
taxonomy_mat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(taxonomy_clean, `length<-`, max_ranks))
colnames(taxonomy_mat) <- c("Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species")
rownames(taxonomy_mat) <- names(taxonomy_strings)
tax_tab <- tax_table(as.matrix(taxonomy_mat))

# --- Read Metadata ---
Kohler.design <- read.table("Kohlerdesign.txt",
                            header = TRUE,
                            sep = "\t",
                            row.names = 1,
                            stringsAsFactors = TRUE,
                            check.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# --- 3. CREATE PHYLOSEQ OBJECT ---

# First, let's find the samples that are common to both the OTU table and the metadata
common_samples <- intersect(sample_names(otu_tab), rownames(Kohler.design))

# Prune the OTU table to only these common samples
otu_tab_pruned <- prune_samples(common_samples, otu_tab)

# Prune the metadata to only these common samples
# (We need to convert Kohler.design to a sample_data object first)
sample_data_obj <- sample_data(Kohler.design)
sample_data_pruned <- prune_samples(common_samples, sample_data_obj)

# Now, combine all three pruned/matched components
physeq_rarefied <- phyloseq(otu_tab_pruned, tax_tab, sample_data_pruned)

# Let's check the result
physeq_rarefied

```


```{r}

# --- 5. ALPHA DIVERSITY ANALYSIS ---

# 1. Calculate metrics (Observed and Shannon) on the rarefied data
alpha_data <- estimate_richness(physeq_rarefied, measures = c("Observed", "Shannon"))

# 2. Combine the new diversity scores with the sample metadata
# The metadata is already stored inside the phyloseq object
sample_metadata <- data.frame(sample_data(physeq_rarefied))

# We can use cbind() to join them, as they are in the same sample order
alpha_data_final <- cbind(alpha_data, sample_metadata)

# 3. Let's inspect our final alpha diversity table
head(alpha_data_final)
```

```{r}
# --- 5.3 ALPHA DIVERSITY - STATISTICAL TEST ---

# Run Kruskal-Wallis test for Shannon diversity by SampleType
kruskal_test_result <- kruskal.test(Shannon ~ SampleType, data = alpha_data_final)
kruskal.test(Shannon ~ Age, data = alpha_data_final)
kruskal.test(Shannon ~ Feed, data = alpha_data_final)
kruskal.test(Shannon ~ Mother, data = alpha_data_final)
# Print the results
print(kruskal_test_result)
```

```{r}
# --- 6. BETA DIVERSITY ANALYSIS ---

# 1. Calculate Bray-Curtis distance matrix from the rarefied data
bray_dist <- phyloseq::distance(physeq_rarefied, method = "bray")

# Let's look at the first few rows/columns of the matrix
print(as.matrix(bray_dist)[1:5, 1:5])
```

```{r}
# --- 6.2 BETA DIVERSITY - STATISTICAL TEST (PERMANOVA) ---

# We need the vegan library for the adonis2 function
library(vegan) 

# Extract the metadata into a data frame
sample_metadata <- data.frame(sample_data(physeq_rarefied))

# Run the PERMANOVA test
# We are testing if the 'bray_dist' matrix can be explained by
# our metadata variables.
set.seed(42) # Set seed for reproducible permutations
permanova_res <- adonis2(
  bray_dist ~ SampleType + Age + Mother,
  data = sample_metadata,
  permutations = 999,
  by = "margin"
)

# Print the results table
print(permanova_res)
```

# --- 1. Load necessary libraries ---
# You might need to install these first: install.packages("knitr"), install.packages("kableExtra")
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# --- 2. Create your data frame ---
# This holds the data from your PERMANOVA results
permanova_data <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("SampleType", "Age", "Mother", "Total"),
  `R² (Effect Size)` = c("10.27%", "7.90%", "20.7%", "45%"),
  `p-value` = c("0.001", "0.021", "0.001", "N/A"),
  Finding = c("Significant", "Significant", "Significant", "N/A")
)

# --- 3. Create the publication table ---
# We pipe the data frame into kable()
permanova_table <- kable(permanova_data, 
                           format = "html", # Use "latex" if you're in RMarkdown/LaTeX
                           caption = "PERMANOVA Results for Beta Diversity",
                           col.names = c("Variable", "R² (Effect Size)", "p-value", "Finding"),
                           align = "lccc") %>% # l=left, c=center
  
  # This adds professional styling
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), 
                full_width = FALSE) %>%
  
  # Add a footnote for significance
  footnote(general = "Significance determined at p < 0.05")

# --- 4. Display the table ---
# In RStudio, this will show up in the Viewer pane
print(permanova_table)

```{r}
# --- 6.3 BETA DIVERSITY - VALIDITY CHECK (PERMDISP) ---

# 1. Run the betadisper test
# We use the same distance matrix (bray_dist) and the group we want to test
dispersion_test <- betadisper(bray_dist, sample_metadata$SampleType)
print("--- Results for SampleType ---")
# 2. Test the dispersion results with an ANOVA
anova(dispersion_test)

# Test dispersion for Age
dispersion_age <- betadisper(bray_dist, sample_metadata$Age)
print("--- Results for Age ---")
anova(dispersion_age)

# Test dispersion for Mother
dispersion_mother <- betadisper(bray_dist, sample_metadata$Mother)
print("--- Results for Mother ---")
anova(dispersion_mother)
```

```{r}
# --- 7. VISUALIZE BETA DIVERSITY (NMDS) ---

nmds_res <- metaMDS(bray_dist, k = 2, trymax = 100)

# 2. Check the stress (lower is better, < 0.2 is good)
print(nmds_res)

# --- 2. Create an Efficient Bar Plot (Relative Abundance, Top N) ---
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Transform counts to relative abundance (solves the y-axis problem)
physeq_clean <- physeq_rarefied

physeq_rel <- transform_sample_counts(physeq_clean, function(OTU) OTU / sum(OTU))

# 2. Agglomerate taxa at the Phylum level
physeq_phylum <- tax_glom(physeq_rel, "Phylum")

# 3. Find the "Top 5" most abundant phyla overall
# We'll use the dplyr package for this, as it's very clean
top_phyla_names <- taxa_names(sort(taxa_sums(physeq_phylum), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5])

# 4. Prune the phyloseq object to *only* these Top 5 phyla
physeq_top5 <- prune_taxa(top_phyla_names, physeq_phylum)

# 5. Create the bar plot using this new, smaller, relative-abundance object
p <- plot_bar(physeq_top5, x = "SampleType", fill = "Phylum") +
  facet_wrap(~SampleType, scales = "free_x") +
  
  # Change the y-axis label to show it's relative abundance
  labs(title = "Taxonomic Composition by Phylum (Top 5)", y = "Relative Abundance") +
  
  # Use a better color palette (optional, but helps)
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired")

# Display the plot
print(p)
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# --- 1. Define the Correct Chronological Order for 'Age' ---
# This ensures the facets are plotted in the correct order
age_order <- c("Fetus", "Newborn", "7+days", "15+days", "20+days")

# We assume 'plot_data' is your "melted" Top 8 Phyla data frame

# --- 2. Create the "Muck" Plot (Individual Samples) ---

# Filter for Muck samples and set the Age order for faceting
muck_data <- plot_data %>%
  filter(SampleType == "Muck") %>%
  mutate(Age = factor(Age, levels = age_order))

# Plot for Muck
plot_muck <- ggplot(muck_data, aes(x = Sample, y = Abundance, fill = Phylum)) +
  # Make bars thinner
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack", width = 0.7) +
  
  # Group samples by Age using facets
  # 'scales = "free_x"' removes extra space for unused sample slots
  facet_wrap(~ Age, scales = "free_x") +
  
  # Set Y-axis limit from 0 to 1.0 (100%)
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.0)) +
  
  labs(title = "Muck Samples: Taxonomic Abundance over Time",
       y = "Relative Abundance",
       x = "Individual Sample") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  
  # Rotate sample IDs on x-axis to be readable
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 8))

# --- 3. Create the "Sterile" Plot (Individual Samples) ---

# Filter for Sterile samples and set the Age order for faceting
sterile_data <- plot_data %>%
  filter(SampleType == "Sterile") %>%
  mutate(Age = factor(Age, levels = age_order))

# Plot for Sterile
plot_sterile <- ggplot(sterile_data, aes(x = Sample, y = Abundance, fill = Phylum)) +
  # Make bars thinner
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack", width = 0.7) +
  
  # Group samples by Age using facets
  facet_wrap(~ Age, scales = "free_x") +
  
  # Set Y-axis limit from 0 to 1.0 (100%)
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.0)) +
  
  labs(title = "Sterile Samples: Taxonomic Abundance over Time",
       y = "Relative Abundance",
       x = "Individual Sample") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  
  # Rotate sample IDs on x-axis to be readable
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 8))

# --- 4. Display the Plots ---
print(plot_muck)
print(plot_sterile)
```

```{r message=FALSE}
# --- 8. Differential Abundance with DESeq2 ---
library(DESeq2)

# 1. Create a subset of our data containing only Muck and Sterile
#    (We'll use the unrarefied, but clean 'physeq_clean' object)
physeq_to_test <- subset_samples(physeq_clean, SampleType %in% c("Muck", "Sterile"))

# 2. Convert the phyloseq object to a DESeq2 object
#    We tell it we want to test the 'SampleType' variable
deseq_obj <- phyloseq_to_deseq2(physeq_to_test, ~ SampleType)

# 3. Run the DESeq analysis
#    This estimates dispersions and fits the model
deseq_results <- DESeq(deseq_obj, test = "Wald", fitType = "parametric")

# 4. Get the final results table
#    This will compare 'Sterile' vs 'Muck'
res <- results(deseq_results, name = "SampleType_Sterile_vs_Muck")

# 5. Let's see the summary of our results
summary(res)
```


```{r}
# --- 9. Assign Taxonomy to DESeq2 Results ---

# 1. Extract the taxonomy table from our phyloseq object
#    We need to make it a data.frame
tax_table_df <- as.data.frame(tax_table(physeq_clean))

# 2. Convert our 'res_sorted' (a DESeq object) to a data.frame
#    We also need to make the row names (the OTU IDs) a real column
res_df <- as.data.frame(res_sorted)
res_df <- tibble::rownames_to_column(res_df, "OTU_ID")

# 3. Merge our results with our taxonomy
#    We'll join them by matching our "OTU_ID" column with the
#    rownames of the taxonomy table
res_with_tax <- merge(res_df, tax_table_df, by.x = "OTU_ID", by.y = "row.names")

# 4. Let's look at the top 5 hits, now with taxonomy
print("--- Top Hits with Taxonomy ---")
print(head(res_with_tax, 5))
```

           intgroup = "SampleType", 
           main = "Otu0019")
